title: DB48X - Modern RPL Calculator

links.label: DB48X - Reviving the spirit of HP calculators

content:
A modern recreation of Hewlett-Packard Reverse Polish Lisp (RPL)

Free software for physical calculators or phone apps.

  • Best scientific calculator today, a modern rebuild of high-end HP-48 and HP-50 calculators
  • Ships as firmware for real hardware calculators including SwissMicros DM32 and DM42 with low-power ARM SoC
  • DM32: ARM Cortex-M33 (STM32U575); DM42: ARM Cortex-M4 (STM32L476)
  • Rich RPL data types and built-in functions with Lisp-level programming power
  • Targets SwissMicros DM42 and DM32 calculator SoCs (DMCP platform)
  • Firmware-style RPL runtime on ARM microcontroller hardware
  • Simulator tested on macOS and Linux
  • Long-term ports envisioned for ARM HP50/HP49/HP48Gii and HP Prime G1
  • Presented at FOSDEM 2023 with an update in 2024

title: HP aC++ Compiler
content:
C++ compiler for Itanium

Cupertino, Hewlett-Packard California Language Lab (CLL), 1998–2000.

  • Wrote the first native Itanium C++ compiler, pre-silicon testing on ski, overriding HP's plans to ship a PA-RISC to Itanium cross-compiler running in the Aries PA-RISC to Itanium dynamic translator
  • Initiated the common C++ ABI effort (Itanium C++ ABI), proposing a shared Itanium C++ ABI with Cary Coutant and meeting engineers from many companies with Daveed Vandevoorde
  • Represented HP at the C++ standards committee for a short period
  • Improved template handling, notably to support the STL
  • Built high-performance, zero-cost C++ exception handling that became the reference implementation and, documented in the WIESS 2000 paper, motivated the common ABI work above
  • Compiler performance improvements, including redesigning the symbol table for scalability
  • Redesigned the compiler build system to harmonise build configuration across the 16 teams working on the compiler, which all used different makefile conventions — a distant ancestor of Make-It-Quick
  • Compiler and OS interaction for Itanium control speculation: recovery/retry for failed speculation needed low-level OS interrupt handlers and compiler-generated code to cooperate; native bring-up uncovered an obscure corner-case speculation bug that made memcpy misbehave and that all earlier testing had missed
  • Contributed to precompiled headers, another compile-time performance improvement

Quote: "An exceedingly sharp engineer" — Mark Mitchell

title: XL
content:
Extensible language designed to evolve

  • Renamed from LX after discussions notably with Daveed Vandevoorde; focus shifted from experimental to extensible
  • Re-implemented on Mozart (itself largely reusing LX code)
  • Inherited advanced generics from LX
  • XL2 — re-implementation with a simplified parse tree (8 node types), still used in XLR, Tao3D, and ELFE; meta-programming friendly
  • XL2 was bootstrapped in three stages (first stage in C++)
  • XLR — Extensible Language Runtime; initially an LLVM-backed dynamic back-end for XL2; became a language of its own

Quote: "Advanced and revolutionary stuff" — Raphaël Manfredi
